extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, petitioners, patent owners, and PTAB litigators involved in AIA trials and related proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for handling institution, consolidation, stays, petitions, oral hearings, confidentiality, timing, and briefing in AIA (PTAB) trials and related copending reexamination/reissue proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution decision when copending reexamination/reissue exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether to institute an AIA trial when the same claims are at issue in a copending reexamination or reissue proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office will continue to determine institution on a case-by-case basis and will not automatically delay proceedings in favor of a copending reexamination/reissue absent facts/circumstances warranting delay. Relevant facts include whether claims challenged by the petitioner were amended in the copending proceeding, the advanced stage of the reexamination (e.g., reexamination certificate issued), or other circumstances showing duplication or inefficiency. Examples of denials where copending reexamination/amendments were dispositive include Intromedic Co. Ltd. v. Given Imaging Ltd., IPR2015–00579, and Juniper Networks, Inc. v. Linex Techs., Inc., IPR2014–00595. The Office does not propose rule changes to enumerate specific stay/denial circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for consolidation of copending reexamination/reissue with AIA trial
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors the Board should consider when deciding whether to consolidate an AIA trial with a copending reexamination or reissue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office and commenters identified multiple relevant factors (not exhaustive): (1) type of additional proceeding; (2) time between filing dates of initial and additional proceedings; (3) stage of the initial proceeding; (4) duration of additional proceeding; (5) scope of each proceeding; (6) whether third-party filers are the same or different; (7) relation between third-party filer and filer of initial proceeding; (8) number of total proceedings filed against the patent; (9) whether the additional proceeding is a reexamination (ex parte reexamination generally should not be transferred to PTAB due to loss of patent owner procedures); (10) whether district court litigation is stayed pending reexamination; (11) whether validity of claims is on appeal to the Federal Circuit; (12) express interests of the parties; (13) issues raised in different proceedings; (14) ability of the Board to reach a timely conclusion in any proceeding; and (15) cost/resource savings from consolidation. The Office will weigh these and other factors on a case-by-case basis and will not adopt a bright-line rule requiring consolidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: How consolidated proceedings should be handled
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures and practices for conducting consolidated AIA trials, or consolidations between AIA trials and reexaminations/reissues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office agrees that consolidation or coordinated handling may be appropriate in many situations. The Board has consolidated inter partes reviews involving the same parties and patents where appropriate (e.g., Ford Motor Co. v. TMC Fuels Injection System, IPR2014–00272). In some consolidations panels have allowed limited additional briefing when different parties take different positions (e.g., Motorola Mobility LLC v. Softview LLC). The Office may coordinate schedules of related proceedings without formally consolidating them, set consolidated trial schedules and discovery, and coordinate hearings (including consecutive-day hearings for related cases). The Office will continue to determine the appropriate approach on a case-by-case basis. No rule change is proposed to mandate uniform consolidation procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entry of claim amendments in consolidated proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether claim amendments should be automatically entered when an AIA trial is consolidated with a copending reexamination or reissue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim amendments are available in all such proceedings, but the Office rejects the notion that all claim amendments should be entered as a matter of right in consolidated proceedings. Entry of claim amendments is left to the panel conducting the consolidated proceeding in accordance with the statutory and regulatory framework applicable to each proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to deny or reject petitions as duplicative
rubrics_metrics.description: Circumstances under which a petition for an AIA trial should be denied because the same or substantially the same prior art or arguments were previously presented to the USPTO in another petition, reexamination, or reissue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office balances petitioners’ interests in presenting new art/arguments against patent owners’ interest in avoiding harassment from repetitive petitions. The Board exercises broad discretion and considers factors such as: (1) degree of overlap between prior art and arguments in the multiple petitions; (2) identity of the later-filed petitioner; (3) whether the later petitioner used an earlier decision as a roadmap to refine/recycle arguments; (4) whether the later petition suggests patent-owner harassment; and (5) whether granting the later petition is in the interests of justice. The Office cites precedents (e.g., ZTE Corp. v. ContentGuard Holdings Inc., IPR2013–00454; Medtronic v. Robert Bosch Healthcare Systems, IPR2014–00436) in which institution was denied under 35 U.S.C. 325(d) for substantially the same art/arguments. The Office will not adopt a rigid "one-and-done" rule binding all challengers to the outcome of a first-filed petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for extending the one-year statutory period
rubrics_metrics.description: Circumstances constituting 'good cause' to extend the one-year period for the Board to issue a final determination in an AIA trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office will continue to strive to complete trials within the one-year statutory period and will not adopt a specific enumerated list of good-cause circumstances into the rules. Instead, extensions will be decided on the facts of each case. The Office will, however, revise the Practice Guide to provide examples of instances where extensions may be warranted (not an exclusive list). Commenters suggested appropriate circumstances including: need for comparative tests; delay attributable to the non-requesting party; existence of later-filed AIA proceedings on the same patent; additional discovery (e.g., on secondary considerations or real party-in-interest); time needed to consider amended claims; unexpected unavailability of an irreplaceable participant; complexity arising from multiple proceedings, many parties, complicated discovery, consolidated/joined trials, or particularly complex inventions. The Office retains discretion to deny extensions to preserve the one-year benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitting live (oral) testimony at the oral hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: When live testimony of declarants should be permitted at final oral hearings in AIA trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests for live oral testimony will be considered on a case-by-case basis and are not expected to be granted routinely; the panel has discretion to permit live testimony when it will be helpful (for instance, on conflicting expert testimony), and to determine the format for presenting such testimony. Live testimony admitted at the final hearing becomes evidence in the record. The Office notes that one motion for oral testimony has been granted to date (K–40 Electronics, LLC v. Escort, Inc., IPR2013–00203).

rubrics_metrics.name: Format of oral hearings and rebuttal practice
rubrics_metrics.description: How oral hearings are structured, particularly whether parties may reserve time for main and rebuttal argument and whether new evidence may be presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office declined to adopt a mandatory main/rebuttal time reservation scheme. Current practice on availability of rebuttal is governed by burdens of proof: the petitioner (burden to prove unpatentability) is permitted to rebut the patent owner’s arguments; likewise, a patent owner presenting argument on a motion to amend may rebut the petitioner’s opposing arguments. Providing a rebuttal to the patent owner as a matter of right on unpatentability would improperly disadvantage the party with the burden of proof. New evidence generally may not be presented at the final hearing unless otherwise authorized, to avoid unfair surprise. The Board retains broad discretion to conduct hearings in the interests of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exchange and limits on demonstratives used at oral argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for exchanging demonstrative exhibits and limitations on their use at oral hearings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office will modify rules to require exchange of demonstratives seven business days before the final hearing date. Guidelines on demonstrative exhibits are intended to prevent supplementing the record with additional evidence or arguments after the evidentiary period has ended, and the Office did not relax those guidelines. Parties may request additional time to exchange and confer on demonstratives; the Office adopted the 7-business-day exchange requirement to address such concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing logistics: recesses, panel attendance, and facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical expectations for hearings, including availability of recesses, panel member attendance, and hearing-room access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests for a recess during oral argument (e.g., to confer with an expert over claim construction issues) will be evaluated case-by-case by the panel. The Office generally ensures that panel members assigned to a particular case are present at the session when that case is heard and encourages participation across multi-session related hearings, though scheduling conflicts may occasionally occur. Hearing rooms are opened to the parties and public 30 minutes before scheduled start times. The Office plans upgrades to enable hearings in regional offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of confidential information and protective order mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: How party-confidential information produced under protective orders is handled in AIA proceedings and the mechanics for motions to seal and protective orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office seeks a balance between public disclosure and protection of truly sensitive information. Under existing rules: a motion to seal provisionally seals information on receipt (Rule 42.14); Rule 42.54 permits orders to protect disclosure or discovery of confidential information; and Rule 42.56 allows expungement of improperly filed confidential information. Parties are encouraged to discuss discovery and confidentiality early and may propose stipulated protective orders. The Office will not automatically enter the default protective order in every proceeding since most evidence is non-confidential. The Office agrees that the party designating information as confidential is in the better position to explain and bear the burden of maintaining confidentiality and will revise the protective order language in the Practice Guide to reflect that burden. Commenters’ procedural suggestions (e.g., conference call to identify opponent’s materials and nexus before filing) were considered; parties may contact the Board while motions to seal are pending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of word counts for main briefing and page limits elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: Format limits for briefing in AIA proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office adopted the use of word counts (instead of page limits) for the petition, preliminary response, patent owner response, and petitioner’s reply brief to gain administrative efficiencies (e.g., streamline petition review and reduce non-compliant filings). For all other briefing, page limits will be maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale rejecting petition page limit tied solely to number of claims or excess claim fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether petition page limits should be determined by the number of claims challenged or tied to excess claim fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office did not adopt proposals to set petition page limits solely based on the number of claims challenged nor to provide automatic page extensions tied to excess claim fees. The Office concluded that number-of-claims alone does not provide sufficient flexibility for a petition to present the precise relief requested and the detailed reasons supporting it.
